The periodic table represents the periodic law, which states that the chemical 
and physical properties of the elements recur periodically when the elements 
are arranged in increasing order of their atomic numbers, Z. This recurrence 
defines the structure of the periodic table, which consists of horizontal periods, 
vertical groups and rectangular blocks (figure 1).

Atoms of metals tend to lose electrons (undergo oxidation) in chemical 
reactions and form positively charged ions (cations). Atoms of non-metals 
tend to either gain electrons (undergo reduction) to form negatively charged 
ions (anions) or share their electrons with other non-metals to form covalent 
compounds. Metalloids have properties intermediate between metals and 
non-metals, so they tend to lose or share electrons in reactions with non-metals 
but gain electrons in reactions with metals.

3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements 
In 1869, the Russian scientist Dmitri Mendeleev published his first periodic 
table, in which the elements were arranged in increasing order of atomic 
masses. To maintain the periodic trends in the properties of known 
elements, Mendeleev left gaps in his table for yet undiscovered elements. 
This facilitated the search for new elements, and all gaps were eventually 
filled. In the modern pericdic table, the elements are arranged in increasing 
order of their atomic numbers, which were identified as a physical property 
by the British physicist Henry Moseley.

Metallic character is a qualitative 
property that cannot be assigned 
a specific value. Most metals are 
lustrous, malleable, ductile and 
good conductors of electricity 
and heat. These properties, 
together with the tendency of 
metals to lose electrons and form 
ionic or metallic bonds, describe 
the term “metallic character”. 
The properties of non-metals are 
generally opposite to those of 
metals, so non-metallic character 
can be defined as being opposite 
to metallic. 
Atomic radii decrease in periods from left to right because the increasing 
nuclear charge pulls the valence electrons closer tothe nucleus. Down a 
group, atomic radii increase because the outer electrons occupy atomic 
orbitals in progressively higher energy levels and thus are further away from the 
nucleus. The increasing size of outer atomic orbitals cannot be compensated 
for by the increasing nuclear charge because the shielding effect of inner 
electrons also increases down a group. 
lonic radii of cations are smaller than those of their parent atoms because the 
number of protons in a cation is greater than the number of electrons, so the 
remaining outer electrons are pulled closer to the nucleus. In contrast, the 
radii of anions are larger than those of their parent atoms because the mutual 
repulsion of the outer electrons increases along with their number. 
Both ionization energy (IE) and electronegativity () increase in periods from 
left to right because both the increasing nuclear charge and decreasing atomic 
radius increase the electrostatic attraction between the outer electrons and 
the nucleus. At the same time, the number of core electrons in the elements 
of the same period remains constant, so the shielding effect also remains 
constant. Going down a group, both ionization energy and electronegativity 
decrease because of the increasing atomic radius and the shielding effect of 
core electrons. 
Electron dffinity (EA) shows no consistent trends in periods or groups, although 
the greatest (most negative) values of EA are typical for elements of groups 16 
and 17. The addition of an extra electron to an atom changes the symmetry and 
stability of the electron cloud, and the change in energy associated with this 
process is difficult to predict. 
lonization energy and electronegativity are closely linked to the metallic and 
non-metallic character of elements. The lower the EA value, the more readily 
the element loses electrons and the stronger the metallic character of that 
element. At the same time, low electronegativity values prevent metals from 
forming covalent bonds and favour metallic and ionic bonding. In contrast, 
high EA values of most non-metals prevent them from losing electrons while 
high electronegativity values favour the formation of covalent bonds. 
The metallic character of elements shows an opposite trend to those of 
ionization energy and electronegativity: it decreases across periads (from 
left to right) but increases down groups. For example, alkali metals (group 1 
elements) become progressively more reactive as their atomic number 
increases. In contrast to lithium, sodium and potassium usually catch fire 
on contact with water (figure 2) while heavier alkali metals react with water 
explosively.

The nature of chemical bonding in oxides defines their physical properties. 
Oxides of most metals are ionic compounds, which are hard, brittle solids 
with high melting and boiling points (Structure 2.7). In contrast, oxides of 
non-metals are covalent compounds with simple molecular structures, so 
under normal conditions most of them are gases or soft, waxy solids with 
low melting and boiling points (Structure 2.2).

Inorganic acids formed in the Earth’s atmosphere from gaseous non-metal 
oxides are responsible for ocean acidification and acid rain. Rainwater is 
naturally acidic (pH 5.5-5.7) due to the presence of dissolved carbon dioxide, 
which forms weak carbonic acid: 
CO,(aq) + H,0(1) = H,CO,(aq) = H*(aq) + HCO,(aq) 
Oceanic water acts as a carbon sink by absorbing carbon dioxide from the 
atmosphere. The solubility of carbon dioxide in water is relatively low, so 
CO,(g) in the atmosphere and CO_(aq) in the oceans exist in a heterogeneous 
equilibrium: 
CO,(g) = CO,(aq) 
When the concentration of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere increases, 
the position of this equilibrium shifts to the right, according to Le Chatelier's 
principle (Reactivity 2.3). In turn, CO,(aq) produces more carbonic acid, which 
lowers the pH of oceanic water and affects the ability of corals, shellfish and 
molluscs to calcify their skeletons. 
Acid rain is caused primarily by oxides of sulfur and nitrogen, which are 
released to the atmosphere by the combustion of fossil fuels (Reactivity 1.3). 
The reactions of these oxides with rainwater produce sulfurous acid, sulfuric 
acid, nitrous acid and nitric acid, which are all stronger than carbonic acid: 
SO,(g) + H,0(1) - H,SO (aq) 
SO,(g) + H,0(1) = H,SO (aq) 
2NO,(g) + H,0(1) = HNO,(aq) + HNO,(aq) 
Sulfurous acid and nitrous acid can be oxidized by atmospheric oxygen to 
nitric acid and sulfuric acid, respectively: 
2HNO,(aq) + O,(g) = 2HNO (aq) 
2H_S0,(aq) + O,(g) —= 2H,SO (aq) 
Strong acids lower the pH of rainwater to5.0 or below, which causes 
corrosion of metal constructions, erosion of limestone buildings, deforestation 
and death of aquatic wildlife.

3.1 The periodic table: Classification of elements 
Oxidation states 
The oxidation state, also known as the oxidation number, shows the number of 
electrons formally lost or gained by an atom in a chemical compound. In most 
cases, the oxidation states can be assigned to atoms using three simple rules: 
* the oxidation state of any atom in an elementary substance is zero 
* inacovalent compound, the oxidation state of a given atom is equal to the 
number of bonds formed by that atom with more electronegative elements 
minus the number of bonds formed by that atom with less electronegative 
elements 
* inany species, the sum of oxidation states of all atoms is equal to the 
charge of that species. 
These and other rules will be discussed in greater detail in Reactivity 3.2, 
where the oxidation states will be used for balancing redox equations. 
Metals of groups 1 and 2 have fixed oxidation states, which are equal to their 
group numbers. Aluminium has a fixed oxidation state of +3. Fluorine has a 
fixed oxidation state of -1 in compounds. The oxidation state of oxygen is =2 
unless it is bonded to fluorine or forms a peroxide. Hydrogen has the oxidation 
state +1 when it is bonded to a non-metal but -1 when it is bonded to a metal. 
The oxidation states of other elements are variable, so they are often specified 
in chemical names by Roman numerals, as shown in the example below.

Transition elements 
Transition elements (groups 3-11) have incomplete d-sublevels in their atoms 
or cations. Zinc and other group 12 elements belong to the d-block but are 
usually not classified as transition elements because they have complete 
d-sublevels in both their elemental state and in all their compounds. 
The first element of group 3, scandium, does not form ions with an 
incomplete 3d-sublevel. However, scandium has one 3d electron in its 
elemental state and, arguably, in some Sc(II) complexes, so its classification 
as a transition element is still debated. 
Many characteristic properties of transition elements are directly related to 
their electron structure (table 2). In the elements of the fourth period from 
Scto Cu, the valence electrons occupy 4s- and 3d-sublevels, which have 
similar energies. As a result, the successive IE values for each of these 
elements increase gradually (figure 5), giving rise to variable oxidation states. 
The incomplete d-sublevels allow transition elements to form complexes with 
various ligands while the electron transitions within d-sublevels are responsible 
for the bright colours of these complexes.

Both elements have their valence electrons in the same energy sublevel (3s) and identical number of core electrons (10), so the shielding effects in both elements are similar. Magnesium has a higher nuclear charge (Z = 12) than sodium (Z = 11), so the valence electrons in magnesium experience a stronger electrostatic attraction to the nucleus than the valence electron in sodium. As a result, the atomic radius of magnesium is smaller than that of sodium, and the removal of an electron from a magnesium atom requires more energy than the removal of an electron from a sodium atom.

The reactivity of halogens decreases down group 17, so bromine is less reactive than chlorine but more reactive than iodine. When bromine water is added to aqueous potassium iodide, elemental bromine will oxidize iodide ions to elemental iodine:
Br2(aq) + 2KI(aq) → I2(aq) + 2KBr(aq)(molecular equation)
Br2(aq) + 2I−(q) → I2(aq) + 2Br−(aq)(net ionic equation)
Depending on the reaction conditions, aqueous or solid iodine can be produced. The solution colour will change from yellow, orange or brown (aqueous bromine, depending on the concentration) to a darker brown (iodine water), and a dark-brown or dark-violet solid might appear (solid iodine). When bromine water is added to aqueous potassium chloride, no reaction will occur and therefore no visible changes will be observed.

The configurations of valence electrons in magnesium and aluminium are 3s2 and 3s23p1, respectively. The 3p1 electron in aluminium is shielded from the nucleus by the completely filled 3s-sublevel, so its removal requires less energy than the removal of a 3s electron from magnesium.
In sulfur, the two paired 3p electrons occupy the same orbital, which increases their mutual repulsion and thus lowers the energy required to remove one of these electrons. In contrast, all 3p electrons in phosphorus are unpaired, and the removal of any of these electrons will break the symmetry of the half-filled 3p-sublevel. Therefore, the ionization of phosphorus requires more energy than the ionization of sulfur.
